claims.text: Wear resistance initially improves as ambient temperature rises.
Wear resistance reaches an optimum at a critical temperature.
Wear resistance degrades rapidly above the critical temperature.
The initial improvement in wear resistance is caused by thermally activated solid-solution strengthening.
Formation of a protective oxide tribofilm contributes to improved wear resistance at lower to moderate temperatures.
At lower to moderate temperatures, thermal energy facilitates formation of a dense, adherent tribo-oxide layer.
The dense, adherent tribo-oxide layer reduces friction and wear.
At higher temperatures, the HEA matrix thermally softens through a reduction in yield strength.
At higher temperatures, the oxide layer may become unstable or spall.
Matrix softening and oxide-film instability cause a transition from oxidative wear to severe adhesive or abrasive wear.
The wear-rate response to temperature is non-monotonic.
Wear rate decreases with temperature up to T_opt and then increases sharply above T_opt.
The critical degradation temperature occurs when thermal softening overtakes protective oxide formation or when the oxide layer loses adhesion.
The critical degradation temperature is expected to lie below the HEA melting point.
The critical degradation temperature is expected to lie above the temperature of maximum oxide stability.

contradictions.description: The intervention says testing begins at cryogenic levels but gives 25°C as the lower endpoint; 25°C is not cryogenic.
